title: Prithu milks the earth: peace for sky and trees
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a king hunts the earth with a bow, and learns to ask her instead
carry: earth, waters and trees are holy; peace starts there
tomorrow: Priya's assembly team is fighting. is there a chant for that?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants weighed sound against sense: Narada knew every mantra and still asked to be taken across. Today, a chant that reaches far past the people saying it.

In the Vishnu Purana, the people of a new king, Prithu, are starving: the earth has held back every plant and grain. Prithu takes up his bow and goes after her. The earth turns into a cow and runs through every world, and everywhere, there he is. At last she turns and pleads: if you kill me, how will your people live? So he lowers the bow, and the earth, like a cow for her calf, gives back every plant and grain. She becomes like a daughter to him, the story says, and that's why she's called Prithivi. Now, a long way from that famine: Priya's rehearsal went badly, and Sam marched her out to the parking lot to look at a tree. It helped, which annoyed her.

`SHE PLEADS. HE LOWERS IT.` → `SHE GIVES, AND IS CALLED PRITHIVI.`

segments.voice: A peace chant from the Yajurveda moves in the same order as that walk outside. Dyauh shantih: the sky, peace. Antariksham shantih: the air between sky and earth, peace. Prithivi shantih: the earth, peace, her name from that story. Apah shantih: the waters, peace. Oshadhayah shantih: the plants, the very ones the earth gave back, peace. Vanaspatayah shantih: the trees, peace. Then it widens, to the gods, to everything, and only at the very end does it turn: may that peace come to me. Here's the teaching under it. In Hinduism, the sky, the earth and the waters aren't scenery. They're holy. The earth is Bhudevi, a goddess and a mother; even a king with a bow had to ask her, not break her. Rivers are goddesses: the Ganga is Ganga Ma, Mother Ganga. Plants are honored: many homes keep a tulsi plant, holy basil, and water it each morning. Some families say a short verse before their feet touch the floor, asking Mother Earth to forgive them for stepping on her. So the chant can't start with me; it walks inward and arrives at one human being last of all. Here's where it meets now. Priya's peace didn't come from fixing the rehearsal. It came from a tree. The chant would say that's the right order: peace for the holy world first, then for me, because I live inside it, not above it.
screen: `SKY, AIR, EARTH, WATERS, PLANTS, TREES.` · `THE EARTH IS A MOTHER.` · `TULSI, GANGA MA.` · `IT ARRIVES AT ME LAST.` · then, large: `PEACE STARTS WITH THE HOLY WORLD.`

segments.voice: If you can, walk slowly to a window or a door. On the way, name each thing as the chant does: sky, air, earth, water, a plant, a tree, even if the water is a glass on the table. At the end, if it's part of your practice, touch the floor with your fingertips, the way many Hindus greet the earth each morning. Then stand still and breathe there until the time runs out.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: dyauh shantih, sky, peace, a chant that honors the holy world before it reaches me.

Prithu.meaning: a just king of the Puranas who 'milked' the earth for his people

Bhudevi.meaning: the earth as a goddess and mother

tulsi.meaning: holy basil, a plant tended and worshiped in many Hindu homes

Yajurveda.meaning: one of the Vedas, the Veda of ritual formulas

prithivi.meaning: the earth; the Purana links the name to King Prithu

notes: Peace chants, day 3 of 4. YV (VS) 36.17 from memory: dyauḥ śāntir antarikṣaṃ śāntiḥ pṛthivī śāntir āpaḥ śāntir oṣadhayaḥ śāntiḥ vanaspatayaḥ śāntir viśve devāḥ śāntir brahma śāntiḥ sarvaṃ śāntiḥ śāntir eva śāntiḥ sā mā śāntir edhi. Spoken in pausal forms (shantih after each noun) for learners; confirm, and confirm the closing 'may that peace come to me'.
Grammar stated: nominal sentences with no verb ('sky, peace'), read as statement or wish. Confirm. 'Vanaspatayah: trees' avoids the 'lord of the forest' etymology.
